About: The Doppler Effect

Source

Topic
Waves — the Doppler effect for sound
Concept
A moving source and a moving observer are not the same thing — at the same speed they give different observed frequencies, because only the source compresses the wavefronts in the medium.
Audience
JEE / NCERT Class 11–12
Serves
Distinguishing source motion from observer motion; the shock/Mach cone as the limit vs ≥ v.
Inquiry
Compare 30 m/s source-toward vs 30 m/s observer-toward and commit to a prediction before the reveal.
Misconception
“Only relative motion matters.” For sound it does not — the medium breaks the symmetry.

Guided Inquiry

The one thing to notice

A source is emitting sound at a steady rate. Move the source speed slider up: the circles crowd together ahead of the source and spread out behind it. Each circle is centred on where the source was when it emitted it — nothing about the circle itself changes after birth.

Watch the two listeners' readings. Then advance.

Predict

Set the source moving toward the ahead-listener at 30 m/s (observer at rest): the reading is 547.9 Hz. Now instead stop the source and move the listener toward it at 30 m/s. Same 30 m/s, same closing speed. What does the listener hear?

Why they differ

Move the source: each new circle is born further along, so the wavelength in the air is genuinely shorter — λ′ = (v − vs)/f₀. Move the listener: the circles in the air are untouched; you simply run into more of them per second.

Set vs = 30, vo = 0 → the ahead listener hears 547.9 Hz. Now set vs = 0, vo = 30 → 543.7 Hz. The 4.2 Hz gap is not rounding: only the first case changed what is in the air.

Outrun the sound

Now push the source speed past 343 m/s. The circles can no longer keep ahead of the source — they pile up into a Mach cone. Ahead of the source there is no observed frequency: the sound has not arrived yet.

The cone's half-angle θ satisfies . This is the sonic boom.

Source moving, observer moving (toward = positive)

v is the speed of sound in the medium (343 m/s). The source speed appears in the denominator — that is where the wavelength-compression lives.

Wavelength in the medium (ahead of a moving source)

Each emission is born one period later, one vsT further along. The observer, if stationary, meets crests at exactly v/λ′.

Mach cone (vs ≥ v)

The source outruns its own wavefronts. No frequency is heard ahead of the source until the cone arrives.

Why source ≠ observer

At vs = 30, vo = 0 the answer is 547.9 Hz; at vs = 0, vo = 30 it is 543.7 Hz. Only the source compresses the wavelength.

The Physics

The Doppler Effect — Bunching in Front, Spreading Behind · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A source emits sound at a steady frequency. Two listeners stand on either side of it, one ahead and one behind. The sim draws the sound as circles spreading through the air and shows what each listener hears.

What you'll learn

  • Why the pitch you hear changes when the source or the listener moves.
  • How to write the observed frequency in terms of v, vs, vo and f₀.
  • Whether moving the source and moving the listener are the same thing.
  • What happens when the source goes faster than sound.
One source, two listeners, all on a line. Sound travels through still air at v = 343 m/s.

What's on screen

  • Wavefront: a circle marking one crest, centred where the source was when it emitted it.
  • Source: the amber dot, with an arrow for its velocity.
  • Listener ahead: on the right, with what it hears printed below.
  • Listener behind: on the left, with its reading.
See itOpen the sim at its starting values. Watch for: the amber source drifting right, circles spreading from it, and a frequency printed under each listener.

Fixed: the speed of sound v = 343 m/s, in still air. Motion is along one line, and the animation runs 40 times slower than real.

03

A moving source changes the wavelength in the air

Each crest travels outward at v, as a circle centred where the source was when it left. The source emits one crest every T = 1/f₀. In that time it moves vsT toward the listener ahead, so each new crest starts vsT further along the line. Ahead of the source the crests are squeezed; behind it they are stretched:

λ′ahead = (v − vs)/f₀    λ′behind = (v + vs)/f₀
A listener at rest meets crests at f = v/λ′.

So a listener at rest hears f₀·v/(v − vs) ahead and f₀·v/(v + vs) behind. For f₀ = 500 Hz and vs = 30 m/s, the wavelength shrinks from 0.686 m to 0.626 m ahead and grows to 0.746 m behind. The listeners hear 547.9 Hz and 459.8 Hz.

See itKeep vs = 30 m/s and vo = 0. Watch for: circles crowded on the right of the source and spread on the left, with 547.9 Hz ahead and 459.8 Hz behind.
04

A moving observer meets the same waves faster

If only the listener moves, the source is at rest and the wavelength in the air stays λ = v/f₀. The crests still move at v through the air, but a listener walking toward them meets them at the combined speed v + vo. A listener moving away meets them at v − vo, which the sim writes as a negative vo.

f′ = (v + vo) / λ = f₀ (v + vo) / v
Positive vo means toward the source.

With f₀ = 500 Hz and vo = 30 m/s, f′ = 500 × 373/343 = 543.7 Hz. That is lower than the 547.9 Hz that a source moving at 30 m/s produced in the last section.

See itSet vs = 0 and vo = 30 m/s. Watch for: circles evenly spaced around a fixed source, small arrows on the listeners, and 543.7 Hz under each.
05

Source motion and observer motion are not equivalent

When both move, the two effects combine:

f′ = f₀ (v + vo) / (v − vs)
For the listener ahead. For the one behind, change the sign of vs.

The source speed sits in the denominator and the observer speed in the numerator. At equal speeds the two cases differ, because sound has a medium: the air is the fixed reference. Only a moving source changes what the air holds. The gap is small at low speed: 0.004 Hz at 1 m/s, 4.2 Hz at 30 m/s, 60 Hz at 100 m/s.

Motions can also cancel. With vs = 30 m/s and vo = 30 m/s, the listener behind moves toward a source that recedes, and hears 500.0 Hz. The listener ahead hears 595.8 Hz.

See itSet vs = 30 m/s and vo = 30 m/s. Watch for: 595.8 Hz on the listener ahead and exactly 500.0 Hz on the listener behind.
06

Faster than sound, the waves pile into a cone

As vs approaches v, the denominator v − vs shrinks and the frequency ahead grows without limit: at vs = 300 m/s the listener ahead hears 3988.4 Hz. At vs ≥ v the source keeps up with or passes its own crests, and the formula no longer applies.

The circles then pile up along two lines that form a cone behind the source. Nothing reaches the air ahead of it, so the listener ahead hears no sound until the cone arrives. The half-angle θ of the cone, measured from the line of motion, satisfies:

sin θ = v / vs    M = vs / v
M is the Mach number.

At vs = 400 m/s, M = 1.17 and θ = 59.0°. The listener behind still hears a lowered 230.8 Hz.

See itSet vs = 400 m/s and vo = 0. Watch for: two amber cone lines behind the source, no sound yet on the listener ahead, and Mach 1.17.
07

Where it matters

  • Passing vehicles. A siren or horn sounds higher while the vehicle approaches and lower once it has gone by. The source emits the same f₀ throughout.
  • Measuring speed. Police radar and medical ultrasound send a wave at a moving target and read its speed from the frequency shift of the reflection.
  • Sonic boom. A supersonic aircraft drags its cone along. Everyone it sweeps over hears the boom, not just those near the moment the aircraft passes Mach 1.
  • Limits of the sim. It models still air and motion along one line. It does not model wind or the changing distance as a source passes a listener.
08

Summary

In one line. The frequency a listener hears differs from the frequency the source emits when the source or the listener moves.

Key points

  • f′ = f₀ (v + vo) / (v − vs), with vs and vo positive when they bring source and listener together.
  • Only source motion changes the wavelength in the air.
  • For vs ≥ v: sin θ = v/vs, and no sound ahead.

Common mix-ups

  • "Only relative motion matters." For sound it does not. The air is the reference, so source and observer motion give different values.
  • "A passing siren changes its own pitch." The emitted f₀ never changes. Only what reaches the listener does.
  • "The boom happens once, at Mach 1." The cone sweeps over listeners all the time the source stays supersonic.

Things to try on your own

  • With vs = 0, find the whole-number vo whose reading comes closest to 547.9 Hz.
  • Set vs = −30 m/s and compare both readings with the starting values.
